Steelyards are largely used in machines for the automatic weighing out of granular substances. The principle is as follows: The weighing is effected by a steelyard with a sliding poise which is set to weigh a definite weight of the material, say 1 ℔. A pan is carried on the knife-edges at the short end, and is kept from tipping over by stays. A packet is placed on the pan to receive the material from the shoot of a hopper. A rod, connected at its lower end with the steelyard, carries at its upper end a horizontal dividing knife, which cuts off the flow from the shoot when the steelyard kicks. When the filled packet is removed, the steelyard resumes its original position, and the filling goes on automatically.

is a poise which can be slid along the upper bar of the steelyard. The steelyard is exactly in balance when there is no weight on the platform and <math>\text{Q}</math> is at the zero end of its run, at <math>\text{O}</math>. Suppose that the weight of the goods on the platform is (<math>p</math>) ℔, and that <math>\frac{1}{n}</math>th of this weight is transmitted by the long body lever to the point <math>\text{A}</math>, so that <math>\frac{p}{n}</math> ℔ is the pull at <math>\text{A}</math>. Let the lower bar of the steelyard be graduated in equal divisions of length, <math>d</math>, each of which represents one penny, so that the distance <math>\text{CA}=q\times d</math> represents <math>q</math> pence. Then the number <math>\overline{p\times q}</math> represents the total value of the goods on the platform. If <math>\text{Q}</math> ℔ be the weight of the poise <math>\text{Q}</math>, the position of <math>\text{Q}</math> when the steelyard is exactly in balance is given by the equation <math>\frac{p}{n}\times q.d=\text{Q}\times\text{OQ}</math>, or <math>\text{OQ}=\overline{p\times q}\times\frac{d}{n\text{Q}}</math>. If therefore the upper bar be graduated in divisions, each of which is <math>\frac{d}{n\text{Q}}</math>, the indication of the poise <math>\text{Q}</math>, viz. <math>\overline{p\times q}</math> graduations, gives correctly the value of the goods. Thus to ascertain the value of goods on the platform of unknown weight at a given price per ℔, it is only necessary to slide the steelyard till the weight acts at the division which represents the price per ℔, and then to move the poise <math>\text{Q}</math> till the steelyard is in balance; the number of the division which defines the position of the poise <math>\text{Q}</math> will indicate the sum to be paid for the goods. When the load on the platform is large, so that the value of the goods may be considerable, it is convenient to measure the larger part of the value by loose weights which, when hung at the end of the steelyard, represent each a certain money value, and the balance of the value is determined by the sliding poise <math>\text{Q}</math>.
